1:
The voices agree on the shape of the arrangement and quarrel over its numbers. Henry describes a new-modelled government: on his accession by conquest Darius made Daniel prime-minister of state, first commissioner both of the treasury and of the great seal, since the dominion was very large and no more can be expected from one man than one man can do. The hundred and twenty princes were given districts in which to administer justice, preserve the public peace and levy the revenue, and over them a triumvirate was set to state the public accounts and to receive appeals or complaints of maladministration. Keil and Delitzsch put the same structure more administratively, that the three chiefs were placed over the satraps especially for regulating the gathering in of the tribute of the different provinces; they add that the word rendered president has no right etymology in the Semitic and is derived from the Aryan, and they report that modern critics have made this arrangement an argument against the credibility of the narrative, since Xenophon has Cyrus appointing satraps to the number of six.

On the count itself Gill has Darius dividing the kingdom of Babylon into a hundred and twenty provinces as was the manner of the Medes and Persians, notes that a later Darius divided Persia into twenty provinces according to Herodotus, and reports that seven more were afterwards added through the victories of Cyrus and Cambyses, and that Josephus through forgetfulness makes the number three hundred and sixty. Clarke has the same enlargement to a hundred and twenty-seven by the victories of Cambyses and Darius Hystaspes, and calls the figure in Josephus most probably an exaggeration or mistake. Ellicott reports that the Greek translators make the number a hundred and twenty-seven so as to agree with the opening of the book of Esther.

The purpose clause divides Calvin from the rest. Some, he says, translate it that the king should not have any trouble, but since the word signifies to suffer loss he willingly adopts that sense: the king did not escape trouble through a desire for ease, as he might have done, being an old man, but willingly managed his own affairs and committed the care of them to three men lest anything should be lost through passing through too many hands, for experience shews us how confusion is caused by a multitude. Henry, who keeps the received rendering, takes the damage more broadly, as covering not only loss of revenue but the abuse of delegated power to oppress the subject, since by that the king, whether he thinks so or no, receives real damage, both as it alienates the affections of his people and as it provokes the displeasure of God. Gill reads the same provision from below, that the people might apply to the presidents for redress of grievances if oppressed.

Why a conqueror should promote a captive is the last question. Henry praises Darius for preferring a man purely for personal merit and fitness for business, though Daniel had been great in the kingdom just conquered, was a native of a foreign and ruined kingdom, and might have been despised as a stranger; he notes too that Daniel was now very old and as able as ever. Calvin makes the promotion providential rather than perceptive: Darius would never have noticed a stranger and a captive unless he had heard how the hand appeared upon the wall and how Daniel denounced destruction on Belshazzar, and God interposed his servant so that the wretched captives and exiles should be benefited, the Persians being barbarians and not naturally more merciful than others. Ellicott suggests only that Darius continued a form of government he found already existing. Wesley recalls that the promise made to Daniel by Belshazzar was of the third rank, the first being general of the army and the second president of the palace.
3:
The preferment is read as a plain excellence. Gill reports a second rendering, that he was victorious above them, and explains it that Daniel got more credit and applause than the rest, being more exact, diligent, laborious and conscientious. Ellicott gives the same sense from the language, that literally he outshone the others, and notes that the pronoun prefixed to the name points him out as the favoured one already mentioned. Clarke reports what the king intended, to make him grand vizier, and adds that this partiality made Daniel the object of the other presidents and the grandees. Calvin turns the promotion into a complaint about his own age. It does not always happen, he says, that those remarkable for prudence obtain greater authority; in the palaces of kings we often see men of brutal dispositions holding high rank, so that audacity and recklessness obtain the highest honours, and we need not go back to history for this. He counts two benefits together here, that a greater portion of the Spirit was bestowed on Daniel, and that Darius was a competent judge of it.

On the search for a charge the voices supply different motives. Gill divides the conspirators: the princes were against Daniel because he was so strict and exact in looking into their accounts that no fraudulent measures could be taken to cheat the king of his revenue, and the presidents because he was preferred above them. Calvin traces it to envy, a vice rampant in all ages, since aspirants to greatness can never bear the presence of virtue, and being guilty of evil themselves are necessarily bitter against the virtue of others; nor does he find it surprising that men who had passed through numerous changes of fortune could not bear an obscure and unknown person set over them. He then watches the vice grow, since nothing is more tempting than gliding down from one vice to a worse: the envious become spies of the fortunes of those they envy, and when they find no crime they trample upon justice without modesty and without humanity.

What the charge was to consist of is the question of the next verses. Wesley reads the phrase as an attempt to make Daniel guilty of treason or other high misdemeanours in the king’s business. Ellicott takes the same phrase of his official capacity, and states the design most precisely: the plan was to place Daniel where his civil and religious duties might be forced to clash with each other, the whole conspiracy being the evident result of jealousy at his advancement. Clarke puts the trap in a sentence. They found no blemish in his administration, for he was faithful to his king, and this was a virtue; but he was also faithful to his God, and this they hoped to construe into a crime and make it the cause of his ruin.

Calvin alone draws the lesson out at length, and he draws two. The first is that Daniel admonishes us by his own example to strive after integrity, and so to deprive the wicked of the occasion they seek: there is no better defence against the envious and the slanderous than to conduct ourselves righteously, for whatever snares they lay, our innocence will repel their malice like a shield, and integrity is the best of all protectors. The second is that the danger came only because Daniel would not leave off the sincere worship of God and its outward profession; from which Calvin concludes that piety is to be esteemed of more value than life itself, and that this temporary life ought not to be more precious to us than the honour of God unstained. He also reads the plot as a deliberate collision with the Almighty, since in plotting against a prophet known to be approved by God they purposely wage war with God himself.
6:
The manner of the approach is noticed before the matter. Gill observes that the word signifies to assemble in a tumultuous and noisy way, and takes it that they thought by their noise, their bustle and bluster, to carry their point, the bill being already drawn ready to be signed. Ellicott reads the same detail as a courtier: such conduct was very unusual in Eastern Courts, where the strictest decorum was preserved, and the breach of etiquette must have prepared the king to expect some terrible crisis in the State.

The claim of unanimity is challenged from three sides. Henry notes that the bill was pretended to be the result of mature deliberation, advised by every rank of officer and carried without a dissenting voice, and answers that Daniel, chief of the three presidents, plainly did not agree to it. It is no new thing, he adds, for that to be represented as the sense of a nation which is far from being so; and he laments the infelicity of kings who, having to see and hear with the eyes and ears of others, are often wretchedly imposed upon. Gill counts heads: there were but three presidents and Daniel was one, so the whole body here amounts to two, and they made the most of it. Keil and Delitzsch dissent on the grammar rather than the arithmetic, holding that the phrase denotes not the three presidents but all the prefects of the kingdom in their four classes, a reading required by the construction and by the missing connecting particle.

On the decree itself the voices set out the bait and the trap. Clarke asks what pretence could be urged for so silly an ordinance, and answers that probably, to flatter the ambition of the king, they pretend to make him a god for thirty days, so that the whole empire should pay him divine honours; that was the bait, the real object being to destroy Daniel. Ellicott finds a political object beside the private one: by consenting the king would acknowledge a system of theology in which he was the living manifestation of all the gods, while his subjects had opportunity of doing him religious homage, which is probably what kept Darius from perceiving any plot. Henry allows it one appearance of good, that it magnifies the king and makes him seem both great and kind, and then takes it apart. It is bad enough to forbid asking a petition of any man, for must not a beggar ask an alms, and if a child want bread must he not ask his parents; but to forbid asking of any god is an affront to all religion, and to interdict prayer for thirty days is to rob God of all the tribute he has from man and man of all the comfort he has in God. The strangest part, he notes, is that rather than fail to trouble Daniel these men deny themselves and their friends the satisfaction of praying to their own gods.

Why the king signed is Calvin’s question. He canvasses two conjectures, that Darius could not bear the glory of his son-in-law, or that he was touched by secret emulation, and finds neither valid; he prefers that at the beginning of a new reign they fixed on something new and unaccustomed, as flatterers of royalty often do. The king, having lately brought the Chaldees under the yoke, wished to prove the obedience of men who had been masters before. Calvin will not excuse him: he does not purposely provoke the gods, but through respect for men he forgets the deities and substitutes himself in their place, as if it were in his power to attract the authority of heaven to himself. If any one could enter the hearts of kings, he says, he would find scarcely one in a hundred who does not despise everything divine.
8:
The pressure to sign at once is noticed by Gill: the conspirators had not merely agreed the substance among themselves but had the thing drawn up ready for signature, and urged that it be done immediately. Ellicott renders the request literally as recording the decree, so that there might be no possibility of its being recalled. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason: they ask for writing so the prohibition might not be set aside, since an edict once emitted in due form and sealed with the seal of the king was unchangeable. Calvin pauses on the word itself, reporting that some render it writing, since laws were formerly graven on tablets of brass, and preferring the simpler sense that what they sought was a signature to a document already written.

What the unchangeable law of the Medes and Persians amounts to is the chief question. Clarke will not have it understood as meaning that whatever laws that people once enacted they never changed, which would argue extreme folly in legislators in any country; nothing more is meant, he says, than that the decree should be enacted, written and registered according to their legal forms, and this one made absolute for thirty days, the laws being such that once passed with the usual formalities the king could not change them at his own will. Keil and Delitzsch reach a similar restriction by another route, arguing against the reading that takes the phrase for the entire national law, as though no law whatever could be disannulled according to circumstances; the word means every separate edict of the king emitted in the form of law, and such an edict was irrevocable because the king was regarded and honoured as the incarnation of deity. Calvin, who does not narrow the phrase, praises what it stands for: fixity sanctions the authority of laws, since when laws are variable many are necessarily injured and no private interest is stable, and where there is liberty of changing them licence succeeds in the place of justice, those who hold supreme power, if corrupted by gifts, promulgating first one edict and then another.

On the mind of the king the voices are of one judgment and different emphases. Calvin sees how inclined to fallacies the minds of kings are when they think they can benefit themselves and increase their own dignity: Darius did not dispute long with his nobles but subscribed, reckoning it might prove useful to himself and his successors if he found his new subjects rather prepared to deny the existence of every god than to refuse whatever he commanded. Gill adds the other motives: the king was moved by the number and importunity of his principal men, chiefly through the affectation of deity the law gave him, and by the chance of ingratiating himself with new subjects, not being aware of the snare laid for his favourite. Calvin also explains the joining of the two nations in the formula by the arrangement of the reign, Cyrus and Darius ruling in common as colleagues, with the greater dignity granted to Darius while the power lay with Cyrus.

Keil and Delitzsch alone defend the decree against a modern charge. It has been called a senseless law which instead of regulating could only break up all society; they answer that it would be senseless only if the prohibition had related to every petition in common life and in the intercourse of civil society, whereas it referred only to the religious sphere of prayer as an evidence of worshipping God, and was altogether reasonable in character if the king was venerated as an incarnation of the deity. They add that since the intention concealed from the king was only to effect the overthrow of Daniel, the law cannot be regarded as an attempt to press a national religion on the nations of the kingdom or to end religious freedom.
10:
Gill begins with what Daniel did not do. He learned of the signature by report or public proclamation, and not until it was signed, or he might have prevented it, having great interest with the king; but the thing being done he did not solicit its abrogation, knowing that vain, nor go to the king with complaints against his enemies, but let things take their own course, determined to be found in his duty. Wesley makes the same point from the other side: he did not abate his prayers for the command of the king, nor did he break the law purposely, since he did no more than he was wont to do in serving his God.

Calvin takes up the objection directly, because he knows it is felt. Only external profession is in question here, not internal worship; and many think the prophet ran great risks without sufficient reason, increasing the chance of death when nothing but outward profession had been forbidden. He answers first that the Spirit speaks through the mouth of Daniel here, so this magnanimity must have pleased God, and the deliverance that followed showed how greatly the piety was approved. Then he answers from the nature of the thing: prayer is the principal sacrifice God requires, so in forbidding it for a month the king exacted from every man a denial of God, which Daniel could not grant without an atrocious insult. Least of all could he change his practice quietly: if he had altered his habits at all it would have been a partial abjuration, that very difference being a proof of perfidious defection. He was in the habit of praying with his windows open, and so continued in his usual course. Calvin closes by rebuking those who deride this as too inconsiderate and simple, since they so separate faith from its outward confession as to suppose it can remain entire even when completely buried, and to avoid the cross depart a hundred times from its sincere profession.

The direction of the face is explained from older practice. Clarke reports that when the Jews were in distant countries they turned their faces in prayer toward Jerusalem, and when in Jerusalem toward the temple, and traces the custom to the prayer of Solomon at the dedication, where he entreated God to hear those in strange lands or in captivity when they turned their faces toward the land given their fathers and the house dedicated to his name. Wesley grounds it in the same place: the temple was where the Lord placed his name and promised to appear and accept his people, all of it a type of Christ, through whom only sinners are accepted. Clarke notices too that he would not shut his windows to conceal himself. Ellicott insists there was nothing ostentatious in it: he takes the prophet to have removed the lattices from his window so as to see as far as possible toward Jerusalem, and then to have continued his devotions as though the decree had never been recorded. He adds that by this time the prophet must have been close upon ninety, yet his faith is as firm and unwavering as that of his three companions many years before.

Keil and Delitzsch read the verse from the standpoint of the watchers. The satraps did not wait long for the expected disregard; it was his custom, on bended knees, three times a day to pray in the upper chamber of his house with the window open toward Jerusalem, and he continued it after the edict, since to discontinue on account of that law would have been a denying of the faith and a sinning against God. On this, they observe, his enemies had reckoned; they secretly watched him and immediately reported him. That is why the place of prayer is described so particularly, to show how they were able to observe him.
11:
The word for their assembling is the one used when they went up to the king, and Henry keeps its force: they came tumultuously together, visiting Daniel perhaps under pretence of business at what they knew to be his usual hour of devotion. Had they not found him so engaged, he adds, they would have upbraided him with faint-heartedness and distrust of his God; for his love they are his adversaries, while he, like his father David, gives himself unto prayer. Gill has them going in a body to the house, knowing his times of prayer and the manner of it, so as to find him at it as aforetime; he reports an older account in which they found a girl and asked what Daniel was doing, and she told them he was on his knees praying in his chamber, and they went and found it as she said. Keil and Delitzsch have them rush in while he was at his supplications, to apprehend him in the very act, and note that the verb means to press in eagerly and shows the zeal with which they went about it.

They alone defend the story as a story. That the watching itself is not described, they say, is to be gathered from the context and does not make the fact doubtful, unless one arbitrarily introduces pretences for throwing suspicion on the narrative, such as asking whether the whole body of satraps lay in ambush, or why Daniel took no precaution.

Calvin returns to whether the trap could have been avoided and answers plainly: if Daniel had prayed with the slightest secrecy he would not have been a victim to their snares, but he did not refuse the prospect of death, knowing the object of the edict and expecting the arrival of the nobles. Against those who plead that one ought not to incur danger rashly, he sets the reproach that would have followed at once — why do you desist from your accustomed habit, why do you close your windows, why do you not dare to pray to your God. He draws from it that snares are prepared for the sons of God however circumspectly they act, and that they ought to be neither too cunning nor too anxious, nor regard their own security so as to forget that faith must be confessed in its proper place and time.

Calvin reads the approach to the king as a second piece of cunning. The nobles come as conquerors, but say nothing openly about Daniel, whom they knew to be a favourite; they repeat instead their assertion about the impossibility of changing the edict, sanctioning it again as far as they can, so the king should not afterwards dare to retract what he had commanded. Gill notices only that they could go straight from the house into the presence, by their offices or by the officer in waiting. Calvin then turns on the vanity that made the trap work: kings desire praise for consistency but do not see the difference between consistency and obstinacy, for if anything has escaped them unconsidered both prudence and equity require them to correct it, whereas when they have trampled on justice they want every inconsiderate command strictly obeyed. Henry makes the same observation from the other end: when men indulge a proud and vain-glorious humour and please themselves with what feeds it, they do not know what vexations they are preparing for themselves, since their flatterers may prove their tormentors. Clarke leaves the argument for the sentence and asks what the den was: either a royal menagerie, like the place in the Tower of London where wild beasts are kept for the pleasure of the king and the amusement of the public, or a place kept for devouring criminals consigned by the laws to that death, which from the case before us he thinks most likely.
13:
The wording of the accusation is what the voices notice. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the accusers do not describe Daniel as one standing in office near the king, but only as one of a foreign nation, one of the Jewish exiles in Babylon, so as to bring his conduct under the suspicion of being a political act of rebellion against the royal authority. Ellicott reads the same addition as calculated to incense the king still further: here was a foreigner who had received the highest favours from the Court, setting himself up in antagonism to the laws of the kingdom. Calvin puts the sting into words. If any Chaldean had dared to despise the edict his rashness would not have been excused, but that a man lately a slave and a captive should despise the command of the king who reigned over his people by right of conquest seemed less tolerable still; the effect is as if they had said that his own masters are under thy yoke, and yet he rebels against thee. The words are harmless in themselves, he adds, but they endeavour to sting their monarch in every way. The simple narrative would have been that Daniel had not obeyed the command in praying to his own God; instead they charge him with pride, contempt and insolence. He notes too that they open the matter freely only now, since an accusation made at the start could have been instantly refuted.

With whom the king was displeased is a small question that divides Gill from himself. He reports that the phrase can be rendered at it, or with him, that is with Daniel, not so much for what he had done as for not doing it more privately; but he prefers the received reading, that the king was displeased with himself for signing so rashly, now finding that he was circumvented by his princes. Wesley agrees in a line, that it was for having made that foolish decree. Clarke agrees with force: well he might be displeased, when through his excessive folly he passed a law which for its ostensible object would have been a disgrace almost to an idiot; and he pictures the day that followed, the king striving by every means to get the law annulled, speaking to his lords in private and going from one to another till the going down of the sun.

Calvin turns the failure into a study of how kings are trapped. They ought to be the more cautious against cunning because they are besieged on every side by perfidious men whose only object is to gain by false representations; but they acknowledge themselves overreached too late, partly through fear and partly through consulting their own credit, so that they prefer offending God to suffering any outward disrespect from men. Darius, he says, was caught between two fears, of disunion if his nobles conspired to make disturbance, and of the charge of levity that would follow a retraction; and so, though he laboured till the setting of the sun, that perverse shame prevailed. Calvin compares him to Pilate, who wished to liberate Christ and was terrified by the threats of the people when they denounced against him the displeasure of Caesar, and draws the rule that when we do not lean upon the help of God we are always compelled to vacillate.

The last approach is described as the first was. Gill has them leaving the king a while to consider, then returning in a body and in a tumultuous way, clustering about him, rude and noisy, and addressing him in an authoritative and threatening manner. Clarke supposes rather that they had first gathered favourable answers from many individuals in private, and calls the assembly that followed a parliament, come now not to seek the repeal of the law but collectively to urge its execution.
16:
Why the king gave way is stated plainly. Gill has him overawed by his princes, fearing they would stir up the people to rebel, and consulting his own credit lest he be thought fickle, so that he ordered the decree executed and delivered his favourite into their hands. Keil and Delitzsch put it as procedure: there being no way of escape, he had to give the command, and the execution followed, by Oriental custom, on the evening of the day the accusation was made; this does not imply it was the evening on which he had prayed, as has been affirmed to make the matter improbable. Ellicott gives the same custom as the explanation of the delay, the sentence being generally executed on the day it was pronounced, which is why the efforts to commute it ran till sunset. He guesses the lions were kept for sporting purposes, and though the form of the den is unknown, thinks the etymology suggests a vaulted chamber.

Calvin reads the scene as the humiliation of a king by his own pride. Darius had thought his authority would be strengthened by this test of obedience, and that he should become superior to both gods and men; now his nobles rise against him and threaten revolt unless he obeys. When kings take too much upon themselves, Calvin says, they become the veriest slaves of their own servants: their favourites adore them and allow them no authority and no freedom to speak, so that no man thrust into the deepest pit and watched by guards is less free than kings. He calls this a just vengeance on men who will not keep the ordinary station of men but wish to become level with God. Darius had forgotten his own mortality and tried to deprive the Almighty of his power, for if God remains in heaven men must pray to him, and the king forbade any man to utter a prayer.

The parting word is weighed by two voices. Calvin notes that it may be read in the optative, as a wish, and does not doubt that Darius really wished it. Clarke hears more than a wish and calls the words affecting: he is thy God, thou servest him not occasionally but continually, therefore he will deliver thee. Daniel now had the same opportunity of showing his fidelity as his three Hebrew companions before him, the lions being not less terrible than the fiery furnace.

The stone and the seals draw the most comment. Gill insists it was not a heap of stones but a single one, large enough to stop the mouth of the den, and dismisses as fabulous the account that there were no stones in Babylon but only bricks, and that angels brought this one out of the land of Israel. He cannot easily say what end it served, since no friend would venture in to make a rescue. Ellicott finds the answer in the distrust of the nobles, who feared a rescue by the king, and who could themselves not reach Daniel if he survived the fury of the lions. Calvin agrees, and thinks it disgraceful that they exacted from their own king a guarantee against the liberation; but he sets a providence over it: the counsel of God arranged that the nobles should seal the stone with their own rings, so that when the king came on the morrow the rings were entire and the seals unbroken, and the preservation was manifestly by the aid of heaven and not the art of men. Clarke reaches the same conclusion: all this precaution served the purposes of divine providence, since there could be no trick nor collusion, and if Daniel were preserved it must be by the power of the Supreme God. He compares the precaution taken at the burial of the Lord, which became one of the strongest proofs of the resurrection.
18:
The night is described by its subtractions. Henry has the king going to his palace vexed at himself, calling himself unwise and unjust for not setting the law of God and nature against the law of the Medes and Persians; he ate no supper, forbade the music, since nothing is more unpleasing than songs sung to a heavy heart, and went to bed but got no sleep, full of tossings to and fro till the dawning of the day. The best way to have a good night, Henry adds, is to keep a good conscience. Clarke lists the same abstinences and adds one, that no sweet odours were burnt or brought before him, and he weighs the age of the sufferer: Darius could not have been less than sixty-two or sixty-three at this time, which shows more fully the depth of his concern. Gill only fixes the hour, that all this was after sunset, since the king had laboured till then, and that it was perhaps late at night.

What exactly was withheld is disputed. Ellicott admits the word is of very doubtful meaning, the root from which it comes meaning to rejoice, but what is signified cannot be exactly ascertained. Keil and Delitzsch do not read instruments of music at all, but take the word as concubines, none of whom were brought before him, supporting it from a cognate in another Semitic tongue; they render the fasting adverbially as going without food in the evening.

Calvin will not let the grief pass for repentance. He calls it tardy, since the king was in the greatest grief and yet did not correct his fault, and observes that this happens to many who are not hardened by contempt of God: they are drawn aside by others and are dissatisfied with their own vices while they still indulge in them. He sets Darius in a middle class. The wicked, having dismissed all fear and shame, revel in their licentiousness; those ruled by the fear of God sustain hard contests with the flesh but bridle their perverse affections; others are between the two, not yet obstinate in malice and not quite satisfied with their corruptions, and still they follow them as if bound by ropes. Such was Darius, who ought to have repelled the calumny of his nobles and opposed them manfully, but who bent before their fury and then bewailed in his palace the conduct he had connived at.

The morning is read as the first sign of a better mind. Gill notices the language itself, that the word for morning is doubled and that one of its letters is written larger than usual, marking not only how early the king rose but his earnestness and solicitude to know whether Daniel was alive. Henry asks how he could lie in bed when he could not sleep for dreaming of Daniel, and has him going in haste himself, since a servant would not sufficiently testify his affection; at the den he cries with a lamentable voice, longing to know and yet trembling to ask, fearing to be answered by the roaring of the lions after more prey. Keil and Delitzsch put the same approach soberly, that he rose at the dawn of day and went in haste, calling with a lamentable voice and feebly hoping that Daniel might have been delivered by the God he continually served. Calvin grants that the king begins here to act with a little more consistency, since the man so struck down by fear as to forget his royal dignity now dreads neither the envy of his nobles nor the perverseness of their discourse, grief having overcome fear. But he refuses to praise either the piety or the humanity of it, because Darius is not yet angry with his nobles until he sees the servant of God perfectly safe.
20:
The cry itself is described before its words. Gill says it was rather like howling than speaking, and that the king cried out before he saw Daniel or heard him speak; Clarke puts it as a physical fact, that a heart full of grief affected his speech.

The title he uses draws the most comment, because it sits oddly on the man who used it. Ellicott calls the phrase remarkable as coming from a heathen king, and then measures the faith behind it and finds it very weak: earlier the king had expressed a vague hope that God would protect his servant, and that hope seems now to have died out, though later in the chapter it appears stronger than that of Nebuchadnezzar. Clarke draws the opposite inference from the same words, that the king was convinced that unless this God saved him the destruction of Daniel was inevitable. Wesley takes the doubt and turns it round: what the king doubted of we are sure of, that the servants of the living God have a master who is able to deliver them and bear them out in his service.

Calvin builds an argument on the title and then refuses what others build on it. If there is a living God, he says, all those imaginary deities whom men fancy for themselves by their own ingenuity are excluded, for deity must be one, and this principle is acknowledged even by the profane: however men may be deluded by their dreams, they all confess the impossibility of having more gods than one, and though they distort the character of God they cannot deny his unity. But he denies that the passage proves, as some allege, the real conversion of Darius and his sincere adoption of true piety. The king always worshipped his own idols and thought it sufficient to raise the God of Israel to the highest rank; and that is too cold, since God cannot admit a companion, being jealous of his own glory, and where he reigns all idols must of necessity be reduced to nothing. Calvin hears the same half-belief in the question itself. The king speaks doubtfully, as unbelievers do, who seem to have some ground of hope but no firm or sure persuasion in their own minds; a secret instinct naturally impels men to fly to God, so that although scarcely one in twenty leans upon his word, all men call upon him occasionally, wishing to discover whether he desires to assist them in their necessities. To ask whether God is able, Calvin adds, is to doubt what cannot be doubted; had the king asked instead whether God had delivered him, that would have been tolerable.

The answer from the den is read by two voices for what it leaves out. Gill notices only that Daniel knew the voice of the king, though the tone of it was so much altered. Calvin dwells on the restraint: Daniel answers moderately and softly, though it was by the command of this king that he had been cast into the cave, and he might deservedly have been angry and expostulated with him, having been impiously deserted by a master who had found him a faithful servant and used his services to his own advantage. When he was oppressed by unjust calumnies the king did not take his part as he ought, and at length, overcome by the threats of his nobles, ordered him thrown into the pit. Daniel might have complained of that perfidy, Calvin says, and does not; he is silent concerning the injury, because his deliverance would sufficiently magnify the glory of God, and he desired nothing except the welfare of the king, which he prays for. Many salute their kings and even their friends in this way through mere form, but there is no doubt that Daniel heartily wished him the enjoyment of long life and happiness.
22:
Which angel it was is answered by three voices with one comparison. Clarke makes him such a one as attended Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego in the fiery furnace and blew aside the flames. Wesley says the same and adds that his presence made even the den a stronghold, a palace, a paradise, and shows how ready angels are to minister to the heirs of salvation. Gill offers two possibilities, one of the ministering spirits, or the Angel of the covenant seen in the fiery furnace and said to be like the Son of God, whom he takes for the Messiah in human form. Calvin cares less for the identification than for the grammar of the claim. Daniel assigns to angels the duty of assistance while the whole power remains in the hands of God, so the angel is the agent and not the author of his safety; and where the Chaldeans spoke indistinctly of their holy deities, Daniel puts forward the unity of God and ascribes the entire glory to him alone, since angels are not moved by their own will but solely in obedience.

On the shut mouths Calvin draws a doctrine of restraint. Lions and the most cruel beasts are in the hands of God and held by his secret curb, so they can neither rage nor injure unless by his permission, and are only so far injurious as he permits in order to humble our pride. He applies it to the fear that outruns the danger, since we tremble at the noise of a falling leaf, and extends it: the God who can close the mouth of a lion will also restrain the devil, who prowls about seeking whom he may devour, and the wicked who plot our destruction.

The claim of innocence is read carefully by Keil and Delitzsch. Daniel declares an innocence which God had recognised and on account of which he sent his angel; and when he adds that he had done no hurt before the king, he means that by the judgment of the king himself he had done nothing wrong, since in transgressing the edict he had not offended against his person. They observe that he could say this the more confidently the more he perceived how troubled the king was, having plainly seen in the transgression no conspiracy against himself but only fidelity toward another God. Ellicott glosses the appeal as meaning that the king knows full well. Clarke puts it in the other order: because he was innocent God preserved him, and now his innocence is fully proved.

Gill gives the gladness of the king two objects: joy for Daniel, alive and unhurt, or joy for himself, being now eased of a guilty and distracted conscience. On the reason given for the preservation, Clarke breaks into a catalogue of what faith accomplishes, the power by which the sea is dried up, the mountains removed, the dead raised, sin forgiven and Satan vanquished. Calvin first weighs the fact that not a scratch or touch was found upon the body, which magnifies the miracle, and is marked more clearly when the accusers are thrown in and immediately torn. He then insists that believing here is not to be taken coldly, as though faith were a confused apprehension of the Deity: it means committing his life to God and reposing on his grace, a fixed determination that his end must be happy if he worshipped him. To show what the word excludes he turns aside to men who fight for good objects and fail, whose ruin he traces not to their cause but to confidence in their own counsels and to ambition, which made them consider their own praise and the applause of the world; from which came the saying of Brutus that virtue is a frivolous thing, uttered because he thought himself unworthily treated in fighting for the liberty of Rome.
24:
Gill limits who was thrown in: not all the hundred and twenty princes and the two presidents, but the chief of them, most busy in getting the decree signed, who watched the house of Daniel and pressed hardest for the sentence. Clarke divides the justice of the act from its extent: it was just that they should suffer the death they had meant for the innocent, but savage cruelty to destroy the women and children who had no part in the transgression. Calvin uses the scene as proof. If the lions were merely satisfied, why, as soon as Daniel was withdrawn, did such madness impel them to tear not one man but a multitude? They would have been content with three or four; instead not one of the nobles was preserved, and the beasts did not wait until their prey reached the bottom but devoured them as they fell. Daniel had been safe among them a whole night; their mouths had plainly been held by divine power.

The edict is measured against an earlier one. Keil and Delitzsch set it beside the decree Nebuchadnezzar made after the deliverance from the fiery furnace and find the same limit in both: Darius acknowledged the God of Daniel as the living God of everlasting dominion, but not as the only true God, commanding him to be reverenced as one who does wonders in heaven and earth, without prejudice to the honour of the others. Henry finds this decree the greater, since the earlier one only restrained people from speaking amiss of this God, while this requires them to fear before him; he calls it a decree fit to be made unalterable, being in substance the everlasting gospel, to fear God and give him glory, and well prefaced with a wish of peace, whose only foundation is the fear of God. But he will not let it stand as enough. Had the king come up to his convictions he would have bidden men not only tremble before this God but love and trust him and forsake their idols; idolatry, however, was too deeply rooted to be extirpated by the edicts of princes.

Calvin presses the objection into a flat denial. He will not take the edict for real piety, as some interpreters do who extol Darius without moderation, as if he had repented; the evidence against it is that his empire was never purged of its superstitions, since he still allowed his subjects to worship idols and did not refrain from the same defilement. What he wished was to set the God of Israel on the highest elevation, which Calvin calls an attempt to mingle fire and water. The profane think they discharge their duty if they merely assign the true God some place and prefer him to all idols; but unless they abolish all superstitions he by no means obtains his right, since he allows of no equals.

How far the address reaches is the last question. Henry allows that all the inhabitants of the earth are obliged to what is decreed, but takes the phrase to mean every dominion of this kingdom, which held many nations and not all; those who have much are ready to think they have all. Wesley says the same in a line, that it means all that great empire, and notes that other rulers are as ready to arrogate the same universality. Calvin traces the actual reach: the king wrote not only for Asia and Chaldea but for the Medes and Persians, since though he never ruled Persia his authority extended there through the alliance with his father-in-law. Gill and Clarke look at the motive: Gill has the king convinced of the miracle and of the omnipotence of God, and Clarke observes that a decree made by a heathen king served to point out the perfections of the true God and the fidelity of his servant.
26:
Gill measures the new decree against the old. It reaches every province, which is what the address to all people means, since to no others could it reach; and it is very different from the decree made days before, forbidding any man to ask anything of any god or man for a month. Clarke takes the decree apart into the characters of God it names: the living God, author and giver of life, all others being dead gods; stedfast for ever, since all things change but he is unchangeable; possessed of a kingdom, for as he made all things so he governs them, and of a dominion without end that no human power can prevail against; a deliverer of those in danger and bondage; a worker of signs in heaven and wonders on earth, showing that both are under his sway; and, to complete all, the deliverer of Daniel before their own eyes. Clarke calls it a fine eulogium. Ellicott notices how unlike a heathen edict the wording is, calling the language remarkably Scriptural and attributing that to the share Daniel must have had in composing it; by the end is meant the end of all heathen kingdoms that shall arise on the earth, the setting up of the kingdom of the Messiah.

Calvin measures the same words and finds them short. Those who take this edict for an illustrious example of piety will say Darius spoke as a herald of the mercy of God; but the king never embraced what Scripture teaches of God nourishing his people with fatherly kindness. He reasons correctly as far as he goes, deriving from one example the doctrine that God can snatch away his people whenever he pleases; but he acknowledges a visible power in a single act without understanding its cause and fountain, that God had chosen his servants and bears witness to being their Father. Unless the hope of deliverance is founded on that gratuitous adoption, any acknowledgment of God will be partial and inefficient. Gill hears a double reference in the words, that God delivers and rescues, as he did the three companions from the fiery furnace and now Daniel from the lions.

The closing notice is read for what it settles. Gill has the same man flourishing throughout the reign of Darius the Mede, continuing a favourite and keeping his posts of trust; he puts that reign at two years, and reports an opinion that it was one only and ended in war, remarking that the authority cited has not a word of the matter. Clarke counts masters instead of years: Daniel had served Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, Belshazzar, Darius and Cyrus, and few courtiers have had so long a term, served so many without flattering any, or left such an example; he asks where we shall find ministers like Samuel and Daniel. Keil and Delitzsch note that the chapter closes as the account of the friends did, adding that Daniel continued in office into the reign of Cyrus, and that the pronoun accentuates the identity, this same Daniel whom his enemies wished to destroy; they deny that the repeated phrase separates the Persian kingdom from the Median, since the word means reign, not kingdom. Ellicott takes the notice as the seam of the book: the first part ends here, having traced these men in their work among the people they lived among as exiles, the miracles all tending to exalt God in the eyes of the Gentiles, while the second part turns to the destinies of the kingdoms of the world. Calvin reads the verb, which properly signifies to pass over and is used here of prospering, as marking a continual possession of honour, and hears a silent contrast between the two conditions of Daniel: obscure through the whole Chaldean monarchy, though all had heard of him as a prophet, and uniformly respected under the Medes and Persians.
